summary: Defines SNMP managed objects for the SMDS Interface Protocol, used to connect to Switched Multimegabit Data Service networks. Here SIP means the SMDS Interface Protocol, not the later Session Initiation Protocol. It was replaced by RFC 1694.

plainLanguage.summary: A list of dials and gauges for checking a connection to a high-speed data service. It makes the readings look the same on any maker's equipment.

questions: how do i monitor smds connections
subtitle: SNMP objects for SMDS Interface Protocol connections

tldr.problem: Network managers needed standardized monitoring objects for SMDS Interface Protocol (SIP), a protocol used to connect to Switched Multimegabit Data Service networks—a high-speed data service popular in the early 1990s.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1304 defines SNMP managed objects organized by protocol layer (Level 3, Level 2, PLCP) and application type (IP-over-SMDS). It tracks counters, error logs, and configuration details at each layer.
tldr.outcome: The SIP MIB became part of the standard SNMP framework for networks using SMDS. It was later replaced by RFC 1694 as the protocol evolved.

facts.label: Protocol layers defined
facts.value: SIP L3, L2, PLCP (DS1 and DS3)

today: RFC 1304 has been obsoleted by RFC 1694, which provides updated definitions for SIP MIB objects. SMDS services have largely been replaced by frame relay and modern broadband technologies, so these MIBs are rarely used in new deployments.

sections.title: Overview of SMDS and SIP
sections.content:
This RFC defines SNMP managed objects for the SMDS Interface Protocol (SIP). Here, SIP means the SMDS Interface Protocol, not the later Session Initiation Protocol. SMDS was a high-speed data service offered by carriers in the early 1990s, delivering switched multimegabit connections to enterprise networks.

The SIP protocol stack operates at several layers. The SIP RFC describes objects for managing SIP Level 3 (the network layer), SIP Level 2 (the link layer), and the PLCP (Physical Layer Convergence Procedure), which adapts DS1 or DS3 transmission formats to the SIP interface. Additional objects defined elsewhere track the DS1 and DS3 layers themselves.

Above these protocol layers, the RFC defines objects for applications like IP-over-SMDS, which allows IP networks to use SMDS as a carrier. A separate document covers SMDS subscription details.
sections.plainLanguage: SMDS was a fast network service from the phone company in the 1990s. This MIB lists the dials for checking each layer of the SIP stack that connects to it.

sections.title: Protocol Stack Architecture
sections.content:
The SIP protocol stack is organized in four layers, each with its own set of managed objects in this MIB. At the bottom is DS1 or DS3, the physical transmission format (managed by separate RFCs). Above that sits the PLCP, which translates between the transmission format and the SIP protocols. The PLCP has separate object groups for DS1 and DS3 variants.

Above the PLCP are SIP Level 2 (the link layer, with PDU—Protocol Data Unit—tracking) and SIP Level 3 (the network layer, with address-based PDU handling). Each layer has its own error reporting and state tracking. The SMDS applications group sits at the top, defining how IP and other services use SMDS.

This layering allows network managers to diagnose problems at each level independently. For example, a badly configured DS1 circuit would show errors at the PLCP level; a broken addressing configuration would show errors at the Level 3 layer.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like a stack of cards. At the bottom is the wire (DS1 or DS3). Above that is a layer that translates between the wire and the protocol (PLCP). Then come two SIP layers. At the top are applications like IP running over SMDS.

sections.title: Managed Objects by Layer
sections.content:
The SIP Level 3 group defines counters and version information for SIP network layer traffic. Key objects track individual and group addressed PDU counts, error counts (including unrecognized addresses and version violations), and the versions of SIP the interface supports. The RFC specifies the version field as a bit mask: a port supporting SIP version 1 and 2 would have a value of 3 (2^0 + 2^1).

The SIP Level 2 group tracks link-layer PDU counts and various error conditions: HCS or CRC errors, payload length errors, sequence number errors, and MID (Message Identifier) errors. A separate PDU Error Log table records the latest occurrence of each type of Layer 3 error, including the source address, destination address, and timestamp.

The PLCP group is split into DS1 and DS3 variants, each tracking Severely Errored Framing Seconds (SEFS), alarm state (no alarm, far-end alarm, or loss of frame), and Unavailable Seconds (UAS). These are standard telecom performance metrics.
sections.plainLanguage: At each layer, the MIB counts how many good messages came and went, and which kinds of errors happened. It marks the time of the most recent error of each type.

sections.title: IP-over-SMDS Configuration
sections.content:
The IP-over-SMDS application group defines objects for managing logical IP subnetworks running on top of SMDS. The protocol (RFC 1209) lets IP networks use SMDS as a carrier for IP traffic. An IP-over-SMDS table entry holds the SMDS address corresponding to an IP address, the group address used for broadcasts on this Logical IP Subnetwork (LIS), and the SMDS address to which ARP requests are sent.

This allows network managers to view the mapping between IP addresses and SMDS addresses, and to monitor the addressing configuration of an IP-over-SMDS service. One SMDS address may be associated with multiple IP addresses, and one SNI (Subscriber-Network Interface) may host multiple logical IP subnetworks.
sections.plainLanguage: When IP runs over SMDS, the MIB lets you see which SMDS addresses go with which IP addresses, and where ARP requests are sent.

sections.title: Error Logging and Diagnostics
sections.content:
The SIP Error Log group maintains a table of the most recent occurrence of each type of Layer 3 syntax error. Errors include destination address format violations, source address format violations, invalid BAsize (Buffer Area size) values, invalid header extension fields, BEtag (Beginning-End tag) mismatches, length field errors, and MRI (Message Receive Interval) timeouts.

Each error log entry contains the interface index, error type, source SMDS address, destination SMDS address, and timestamp. When an error is cleared or never occurs, the timestamp is zero. This log helps network operators diagnose SMDS connectivity and configuration problems.
sections.plainLanguage: When something goes wrong at the network layer, the MIB remembers the last time each kind of error happened, what addresses were involved, and when.
